enrichment.introSourceText: Reading this chapter transparently — without the smoothing most translations apply — reveals features of the source text that are usually invisible.
enrichment.introAneParallels: The world that produced this text was not empty of other stories. Neighboring cultures told their own accounts of how things began.
enrichment.introHistorical: What do we actually know about the world this text describes?
enrichment.introLinguistic: The Hebrew words themselves carry layers that translation inevitably compresses.
enrichment.introScientific: Modern science describes the natural world very differently from this ancient text. Neither validates nor invalidates the other — they answer different questions.
enrichment.introReception: This text has been read for thousands of years. Different communities have heard different things in it.
enrichment.introCuriosities: Some things in the text are simply striking — not because they prove anything, but because they make you pause.

landing.languageTagline: The Bible → English · Português · Deutsch · Español
landing.hook: See what the text actually says — before anyone tells you what it means.
landing.conventionalVerse: Now the serpent was more crafty than any of the wild animals the LORD God had made. He said to the woman, "Did God really say, 'You must not eat from any tree in the garden'?"
landing.transparentVerse: And the serpent was *arum* (crafty/shrewd) from all the living things of the field that YHWH God had made. And it said to the woman: "Indeed, *did* God say, 'You shall not eat from any tree of the garden'?"
landing.diff1: The Hebrew has four consonants: YHWH. 'The LORD' is a substitution tradition — not what the text says.
landing.diff2: The Hebrew word *arum* connects to 'naked' (*arom*) in the previous verse — a wordplay most translations hide.
landing.diff3: The serpent overstates the restriction. The woman corrects it — but slightly changes the original command too. The TT preserves both distortions.
landing.diff4: Italics show every word added for English grammar. You see where the translation ends and the scaffolding begins.
landing.howReading: Reading — continuous prose, clean page, just the text flowing. Read it like a story.
landing.howStudy: Study — verse by verse with color-coded notes. See the Hebrew, the ambiguity, the choices we made and why.
landing.howExplore: Explore — narrative summaries of the scholarship. Ancient parallels, historical context, and open questions presented as flowing prose.
landing.howContext: Context — every scholarly claim labeled by type and confidence. Source text features, ANE parallels, science, later reception. You assess; we present.
landing.howProphecy: Prophecies — what the text predicts, how Jewish, Christian, and Islamic traditions read it, and whether it's considered fulfilled. Every reading labeled.
landing.who1: If you've never opened a Bible and want to know what it actually says before deciding what you think.
landing.who2: If you've read it a hundred times and want to see what your translation smoothed over.
landing.who3: If you study ancient texts and want a translation that shows its work — every choice visible, nothing hidden.
landing.scope: A translation of the Hebrew Bible and Greek Scriptures. In English, Portuguese, German, and Spanish. Governed by 29 rules. It is not a devotional. It is not a replacement for scholarly editions. It is a disciplined attempt at transparency.
landing.scopeNot: It is honest about what it doesn't know.
landing.rulesPageSubtitle: The governance system behind the Transparent Translation.
landing.rulesIntro: Every translation makes choices. Most hide them. We wrote ours down.
landing.rulesPrimeDesc: If any rule conflicts with these four principles, the principles win.
landing.rulesPrime1: Do not simplify what the source text keeps complex.
landing.rulesPrime2: Do not clarify what the source text leaves ambiguous.
landing.rulesPrime3: Do not add what the source text does not say — unless target grammar absolutely requires it.
landing.rulesPrime4: When addition is unavoidable, signal it clearly.
landing.rule1short: Same source word → same translation, by default.
landing.rule1example: Hebrew אֶרֶץ (eretz) always → 'land.' Greek εκκλησία (ekklesia) → 'assembly,' not 'church.'
landing.rule2short: If source text supports two meanings, preserve both.
landing.rule3short: Don't sneak in later concepts not in the source text.
landing.rule3example: Hebrew: 'sky' not 'Heaven.' Greek: 'assembly' not 'church.' 'Good news' not 'Gospel.'
landing.rule4short: Transliterate when translation would impose a single reading.
landing.rule5short: Core terms locked across the project.
landing.rule6short: When traditions conflict, source text governs.
landing.rule7short: Repeated phrases rendered identically each time.
landing.rule8short: Preserve tense, aspect, and voice from source.
landing.rule11short: Mark every word not in the source text.
landing.rule11example: 'And God saw that *it was* good' — italics show 'it was' is added for English grammar.
landing.rule12short: Preserve source sentence structure where possible.
landing.rule13short: Flag debated terms with confidence labels.
landing.rule14short: Note sound patterns and textual echoes.
landing.rule15short: Translation must work when read aloud.
landing.rule16short: All 4 target languages render the same source consistently.
landing.rule17short: Same source passage → same rendering across books.
landing.rule19short: When rules conflict, explicit priority order applies.
landing.rule21short: Commentary belongs in notes, not in translation.
landing.rule22short: Translate base text; note variants, don't adopt silently.
landing.rule23short: Respect the genre of each passage.
landing.rule24short: Transparent vs Reader edition, declared explicitly.
landing.rule25example: YHWH — because that is what the Hebrew consonants are. The vowels were never written.
landing.rule26short: Significant variants noted in companion material.
landing.rule28short: No verse ships without documented review.
landing.rule29short: Companion material in separate files, labeled by type and confidence.
